What is paper trading?

Paper trading means placing trades with simulated money at real market prices. Every part of the experience is real except the risk: you pick an entry, choose leverage, set a stop-loss, watch the P&L move at the live price, and — if you oversize — get liquidated exactly the way a real futures account would. The name is a relic from the pre-computer era, when practice trades were literally tracked on paper.

Brokers call the same thing a demo account; prop firms call it simulated trading. It is all one idea: build skill where mistakes are free, because in a live account the market charges full tuition for every lesson.

How to paper trade like it matters

The biggest criticism of paper trading is real: with nothing at stake, people practice bad habits. The fix is to practice under rules:

1. Trade a size you would actually trade

If your future real account is $500, do not swing $50,000 paper positions. Set the position size you will genuinely use, and treat the demo balance as if withdrawing it took a year.

2. Write the plan before the entry

Entry, stop, target, and the reason — before you click. MarginPad puts risk/reward and position-size calculators one tab away, and the built-in journal keeps every ticket so you cannot rewrite history.

3. Respect the sample size

Ten trades prove nothing. Run at least 30-50 closed trades with the same ruleset before judging it. The win-rate calculator and backtester tell you whether the edge is real or luck.

4. Lose properly

The most valuable paper trades are the losses — they cost nothing and teach the most. Get liquidated at 100x once, on purpose, and you will never need the lesson again. Watch the live liquidations feed to see what happens to traders who skipped it.

5. Graduate slowly

When your sample is profitable and your rules held, go live with a fraction of your intended size — the emotions of real money are the one thing no simulator can rehearse.

Normally no — simulators pay nothing. MarginPad is the exception: weekly leaderboards pay real USDT prizes and daily missions credit real cents for practicing. Learning-sized amounts, honestly framed — the point is that practice stops being unpaid work.
How long should I paper trade before going live?
Count trades, not weeks: 30-50 closed trades with a written plan, positive expectancy over the sample, and no broken rules is a solid graduation bar.

Here, yes: live prices, the same isolated-margin liquidation formula real exchanges use, and realistic fees. The one thing no simulator can copy is the emotion of real money — which is exactly why you graduate slowly.
